content: The Standard for the Uniform Scheduling of Drugs and Poisons (SUSDP) is a regulatory document used in Australia to manage the classification and control of drugs and poisons. It is developed by the National Drugs and Poisons Scheduling Committee (NDPSC), which operates under the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA). The SUSDP aims to standardize the scheduling, packaging, and labeling of substances across Australia, although the implementation of these regulations is ultimately the responsibility of individual state governments. The SUSDP serves as a recommendation to the states, and as a result, variations in drug and poison regulations exist between Australian states. Schedules Overview Schedule 1 (Defunct) This schedule is no longer in use. Schedule 2: Pharmacy Medicine Schedule 2 (S2) substances, also known as Pharmacy Medicines, are therapeutic agents that are generally safe for use. However, they are intended for minor ailments or symptoms that can be easily recognized by consumers and do not require medical diagnosis or management. Pharmacist advice or counseling is available if necessary. Examples include dextromethorphan. These substances can be stored in any part of a pharmacy, except near food. Schedule 3: Pharmacist Only Medicine Schedule 3 (S3) substances, also known as Pharmacist Only Medicines, are therapeutic agents that are generally safe but require professional advice or counseling from a pharmacist. These substances are used for conditions that can be identified by the consumer but may require verification by a pharmacist. They do not require ongoing medical management but may need initial medical diagnosis. Some states have subsets of Schedule 3 with additional requirements. Examples include orlistat, pseudoephedrine, and salbutamol (Ventolin/Asmol). Schedule 4: Prescription Only Medicine/Animal Prescription Remedy Schedule 4 (S4) substances, also known as Prescription Only Medicines, are therapeutic agents that require professional medical, dental, or veterinary management or monitoring. These are used for conditions that necessitate professional diagnosis and management. They may include new therapeutic substances or those requiring further evaluation for safety or efficacy. Some states have subsets of Schedule 4 with additional requirements. Examples include adrenaline, co-amoxiclav, co-trimoxazole, benzodiazepines (except flunitrazepam and temazepam), ephedrine, ergotamine, fluticasone, isotretinoin, pseudoephedrine in large doses, salmeterol, and tretinoin. Schedule 5: Caution Schedule 5 (S5) substances are those with low toxicity or low concentration, presenting a low to moderate hazard. They are capable of causing only minor adverse effects in normal use but require caution in handling, storage, or use. Schedule 6: Poison Schedule 6 (S6) substances are those with moderate to high toxicity. They may cause death or severe injury if ingested, inhaled, or come into contact with the skin or eyes. Schedule 7: Dangerous Poison Schedule 7 (S7) substances are highly to extremely toxic. They can cause death or severe injury even at low exposures. These substances require special precautions in their manufacture, handling, or use and may be subject to special regulations restricting their availability, possession, or use. They are considered too hazardous for domestic use or use by untrained individuals. Schedule 8: Controlled Drug Schedule 8 (S8) substances, also known as Controlled Drugs, are therapeutic agents that are dependence-producing and have a high potential for abuse or misuse. Examples include most barbiturates, buprenorphine, cocaine, dexamphetamine, flunitrazepam, temazepam, methadone, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, morphine, and hydromorphone. Schedule 9: Prohibited Substance Schedule 9 (S9) substances are those that, by law, may only be used for research purposes. Their sale, distribution, use, and manufacture are strictly prohibited under the law. Examples include cannabis, GHB, heroin, LSD, mescaline, MDMA (ecstasy), psilocin, and psilocybin. Interstate Variations New South Wales (NSW) In New South Wales, poisons are listed in the Poisons List by the Poisons Advisory Committee under the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 1966 (NSW). NSW legislation refers to S2 as medicinal poisons, S3 as potent substances, S4 as restricted substances, and S8 as drugs of addiction. Schedule 3 Recordable (S3R) Schedule 3 Recordable (S3R), or recordable potent substances, refers to Pharmacist Only Medicines where supply is recorded similarly to Schedule 4 drugs. These substances have an increased risk of illegal diversion or abuse. As of January 2006, all pseudoephedrine-containing preparations are classified as S3R. Schedule 4 Appendix D (S4D) Schedule 4 Appendix D (S4D) refers to Prescription Only Medicines that do not meet the criteria for S8 classification but still carry a significant risk of addiction or abuse. These drugs are subject to additional prescription and recording requirements compared to standard S4 substances. Examples include benzodiazepines and anabolic steroids. A subset of Appendix D substances, known as Appendix B substances, are subject to similar requirements as S8 drugs. South Australia (SA) In South Australia, certain S3 preparations listed in Schedule G of the Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 1996 (SA) are recordable under Regulation 14(2). As of 2006, Schedule G products include adrenaline (in metered aerosols), dihydrocodeine (in cough preparations), doxylamine (in preparations also containing codeine), promethazine (in preparations also containing codeine), and pseudoephedrine. Western Australia (WA) In Western Australia, certain S3 preparations listed in Appendix J of the Poisons Regulations 1965 (WA) are recordable under Regulation 35A. As of 2006, Appendix J products include hydrocortisone, hydrocortisone acetate, pseudoephedrine, and nicotine preparations classified under Schedule 3.
